claims.source: This was consistent with intracellular square pulse current injections showing no clear HYP after AP firing (Figure 2d).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 2d showing the experimental data.

claims.claim: Motoneuron AP and HYP amplitudes (relative to resting membrane potential) were significantly larger during VOC activity than following antidromic activation at threshold for AP firing (AP: vocal 29.13 ± 1.48 mV vs. antidromic: 21.46 ± 2.93 mV; p=0.024; HYP: vocal −10.92 ± 1.16 mV vs. antidromic −2.95 ± 0.70 mV; n = 12, N = 5: p=0.001).
claims.source: Motoneuron AP and HYP amplitudes (relative to resting membrane potential [RMP]) were significantly larger during VOC activity than following antidromic activation at threshold for AP firing (AP: vocal 29.13 ± 1.48 mV vs. antidromic: 21.46 ± 2.93 mV; p=0.024; HYP: vocal −10.92 ± 1.16 mV vs. antidromic −2.95 ± 0.70 mV; n = 12, N = 5: p=0.001, see Figure 2c).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data (p=0.024 and p=0.001) and reference to Figure 2c.

claims.claim: At low amplitudes of antidromic stimulation, small depolarizations were detected whose amplitude gradually increased with stimulation strength, with shapes and peak latencies indicative of electrotonic coupling (3.54 ± 0.28 ms; n = 9, N = 4).
claims.source: At low amplitudes, we detected small depolarizations (Figure 3) whose amplitude gradually increased with stimulation strength, that is, with increasing recruitment of motoneuron axons and with shapes and peak latencies indicative of electrotonic coupling (3.54 ± 0.28 ms; n = 9, N = 4).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 3 showing the experimental data.

claims.claim: Collision experiments using antidromic-activated and intracellular-evoked APs revealed these APs could not be blocked, indicating they resulted from electrical coupling.
claims.source: Collision experiments using antidromic-activated and intracellular-evoked APs (via intracellular current injection) revealed these APs could not be blocked, that is, they resulted from electrical coupling (Pappas and Bennett, 1966; Kiehn and Tresch, 2002, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Pappas and Bennett, 1966 and Kiehn and Tresch, 2002, and reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: With increasing amplitude of vocal nerve stimulation, the axon of the respectively recorded motoneuron was eventually recruited and an antidromic AP invaded the recorded motoneuron with a significantly shorter peak latency (1.42 ± 0.31 ms after stimulation; n = 11, N = 4) compared to the subthreshold depolarization (p=0.003).
claims.source: With increasing amplitude of vocal nerve stimulation, the axon of the respectively recorded motoneuron was eventually recruited and an antidromic AP invaded the recorded motoneuron as shown by the significantly shorter peak latency (1.42 ± 0.31 ms after stimulation; n = 11, N = 4) compared to the previously mentioned subthreshold depolarization (p=0.003) (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data (p=0.003) and reference to Figure 3.

claims.claim: Antidromic APs showed no HYP, but instead were characterized by a slow decay (double exponential fit; average time constant τ1: 0.89 ± 0.25; time constant τ2: 7.76 ± 2.48; n = 5, N = 2) back to the RMP.
claims.source: These APs showed no HYP, but instead were characterized by a slow decay (double exponential fit; average time constant τ1: 0.89 ± 0.25; time constant τ2: 7.76 ± 2.48; n = 5, N = 2) back to the RMP (example shown in magenta trace in Figure 3a).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 3a showing the experimental data.

claims.claim: The AP and HYP peak amplitudes increased with stimulation strength until each reached a plateau.
claims.source: The AP and HYP peak amplitudes increased with stimulation strength until each reached a plateau (Figure 3a).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 3a showing the experimental data.

claims.claim: A HYP was never observed during intracellular square pulse current injections.
claims.source: A HYP was never observed during intracellular square pulse current injections (Figure 2d), raising the question on the origin of this HYP.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 2d showing the experimental data.

claims.claim: Phase plane plots revealed an additional component: a broadening of the depolarization after AP firing.
claims.source: Phase plane plots further revealed an additional component: a broadening of the depolarization after AP firing (magenta arrows, (Figure 3a)).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 3a showing the experimental data.

claims.claim: A Renshaw cell-like recurrent inhibition could be ruled out as the origin of the HYP given the lack of motoneuron axon collaterals and the rapid onset of the HYP.
claims.source: A Renshaw cell-like recurrent inhibition in which spinal motoneurons use an axon collateral to activate a local inhibitory circuit (Renshaw, 1941; Eccles et al., 1954), comparable to the 'apparently recurrent inhibition' proposed by Pappas and Bennett, 1966 to account for inhibitory input to the VMN, could be ruled out as the origin of the HYP given the lack of motoneuron axon collaterals (Figure 1d, Chagnaud and Bass, 2014) and the rapid onset of the HYP.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from anatomical observations (lack of axon collaterals) and physiological data (rapid HYP onset), supported by citations to Renshaw, 1941; Eccles et al., 1954; Pappas and Bennett, 1966; Chagnaud and Bass, 2014, and reference to Figure 1d.

claims.claim: There was no difference in HYP amplitude (% of baseline) between cut and uncut recordings during VOCs (before cut: −8.21 ± 3.1 mV vs. after: −7.51 ± 1.22 mV; n = 18, N = 2: p=0.8).
claims.source: There was no difference in HYP amplitude (% of baseline) between cut and uncut recordings during VOCs (before cut: −8.21 ± 3.1 mV vs. after: −7.51 ± 1.22 mV; n = 18, N = 2: p=0.8) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data (p=0.8) and reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: There was no difference in HYP amplitude during antidromic stimulation after dorsal root cut (before cut: −3.2 ± 0.59 mV vs. after: −4.84 ± 0.71 mV, n = 18, N = 2: p=0.117).
claims.source: or during antidromic stimulation (before cut: −3.2 ± 0.59 mV vs. after: −4.84 ± 0.71 mV, n = 18, N = 2: p=0.117).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data (p=0.117).

claims.claim: These results excluded a motoneuronal collateral via one of the dorsal roots as the origin of the HYP.
claims.source: These results excluded a motoneuronal collateral via one of the dorsal roots as the origin of the HYP.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental results showing no difference in HYP after dorsal root cut.

claims.claim: Contralateral antidromic stimulation revealed electrotonic potentials whose amplitude depended on stimulation strength.
claims.source: Contralateral antidromic stimulation also revealed electrotonic potentials whose amplitude depended on stimulation strength (ad-contra, red traces; Figure 3a).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 3a showing the experimental data.

claims.claim: The peak latency of contralaterally evoked APs was significantly longer (3.47 ± 0.16 ms; n = 11, N = 4; p=0.004) than ones elicited ipsilaterally.
claims.source: The peak latency of these APs was significantly longer (3.47 ± 0.16 ms; n = 11, N = 4; p=0.004) than ones elicited ipsilaterally (Figure 3b)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data (p=0.004) and reference to Figure 3b.

claims.claim: The peak latency of the ipsilaterally evoked subthreshold depolarization did not differ from contralateral, consistent with their common origin from electrotonic coupling.
claims.source: while the peak latency of the ipsilaterally evoked subthreshold depolarization did not differ, consistent with their common origin from electrotonic coupling (see above).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing similar latencies.

claims.claim: Electrical coupling alone is able to drive AP firing, independent of whether motoneurons belong to the ipsilateral or contralateral VMN population.
claims.source: As tract tracing and intracellular neuron fills showed that motoneurons only innervate the ipsilateral muscle (Chagnaud and Bass, 2014), electrical coupling alone is thus able to drive AP firing, independent of whether motoneurons belong to the ipsilateral or contralateral VMN population.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from anatomical data (motoneurons only innervate ipsilateral muscle) and physiological observations, supported by citation to Chagnaud and Bass, 2014.

claims.claim: An HYP component could clearly be distinguished in the contralateral antidromic stimulation experiments.
claims.source: As with the ipsilateral antidromic activation, an HYP component could clearly be distinguished in the contralateral antidromic stimulation experiments (Figure 4a).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 4a showing the experimental data.

claims.claim: The HYP occurred independent of AP firing, emphasizing the independence of the two events within a given motoneuron.
claims.source: This HYP occurred independent of AP firing, emphasizing the independence of the two events within a given motoneuron.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental observations.

claims.claim: Intracellular current injections failed to initiate an AP in most cases, even at high current intensities (>5 nA).
claims.source: Consistent with our findings in the closely related midshipman toadfish, Porichthys notatus (Chagnaud et al., 2012), the ability to initiate an AP via electrotonic coupling was in strong contrast to our intracellular current injections that failed to initiate an AP in most cases, even at high current intensities (>5 nA).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Chagnaud et al., 2012 and experimental observations.

claims.claim: In cases where intracellular current injection elicited an AP, motoneurons showed rapid adaptation of AP firing, likely due to weak somatic repolarization ability.
claims.source: In cases where intracellular current injection elicited an AP, motoneurons showed rapid adaptation of AP firing, likely due to weak somatic repolarization ability (see Figure 2d).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental observations shown in Figure 2d.

claims.claim: Motoneurons showed no signs of AP adaptation to pulse trains with brief (<5 ms) pulses, indicating the necessity of membrane repolarization for sustained motoneuron firing.
claims.source: In contrast to long (>50 ms) duration pulses (Figure 2d), motoneurons showed no signs of AP adaptation to pulse trains with brief (<5 ms) pulses, indicating the necessity of membrane repolarization for sustained motoneuron firing (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 2d and Figure 3—figure supplement 3 showing the experimental data.

claims.claim: Stimulation was reliable into the behaviorally relevant physiological range with train frequencies tested up to 110 Hz.
claims.source: Stimulation was reliable into the behaviorally relevant physiological range (the PRR/fundamental frequency of toadfish vocalizations) with train frequencies tested up to 110 Hz.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data.

claims.claim: The weak repolarization capability and low excitability of the motoneurons provide the means to prevent sustained AP firing, which would decrease the extent of firing synchrony and precision across the VMN population.
claims.source: The weak repolarization capability and low excitability of the motoneurons thus provide the means to prevent sustained AP firing, which would decrease the extent of firing synchrony and precision across the VMN population.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental observations.

claims.claim: The presence of the HYP only at high antidromic stimulation amplitudes strongly suggested a network-dependent activation of the HYP.
claims.source: The presence of the HYP only at high antidromic stimulation amplitudes, that is, high levels of motoneuron recruitment, strongly suggested a network-dependent activation of the HYP.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental observations.

claims.claim: Once close to the antidromic AP, an HYP started to appear that increased in amplitude the closer the contralateral-evoked potential came to the ipsilateral-evoked antidromic AP.
claims.source: Once close to the antidromic AP, an HYP started to appear that increased in amplitude the closer the contralateral-evoked potential came to the ipsilateral-evoked antidromic AP (Figure 4b; heat map in Figure 4a; also see Video 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 4a, 4b and Video 1 showing the experimental data.

claims.claim: These experiments suggested that an increase in overall depolarization in the vocal network is needed to generate the HYP.
claims.source: These experiments suggested that an increase in overall depolarization in the vocal network is needed to generate the HYP.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental results.

claims.claim: With decreasing lag between the antidromically evoked potential and the depolarization during the VOC, an HYP started to appear in the contralateral-evoked potential that increased in amplitude.
claims.source: With decreasing lag between the antidromically evoked potential and the depolarization during the VOC, an HYP started to appear in the contralateral-evoked potential that increased in amplitude (Figure 4c, d).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 4c, d showing the experimental data.

claims.claim: This again showed the necessity of a network-wide depolarization in order to elicit the HYP.
claims.source: This again showed the necessity of a network-wide depolarization in order to elicit the HYP.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental results.

claims.claim: After intracellular iontophoresis of QX314, motoneurons exhibited a small, but significant, decrease in AP amplitude compared to baseline conditions during VOCs (baseline: 31 ± 2.67 mV vs. QX314: 27.27 ± 2.53 mV; n = 7, N = 2; p=0.015).
claims.source: After intracellular iontophoresis of QX314, motoneurons exhibited a small, but significant, decrease in AP amplitude compared to baseline conditions during VOCs (Figure 5a) (baseline: 31 ± 2.67 mV vs. QX314: 27.27 ± 2.53 mV; n = 7, N = 2; p=0.015).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data (p=0.015) and reference to Figure 5a.

claims.claim: There was a much more prominent decrease in antidromically evoked AP amplitude relative to baseline after QX314 injection (baseline: 21.92 ± 7.16 mV vs. QX314: 8.90 ± 6.82 mV; n = 7, N = 2; p=0.006).
claims.source: There was a much more prominent decrease in antidromically evoked AP amplitude relative to baseline (baseline: 21.92 ± 7.16 mV vs. QX314: 8.90 ± 6.82 mV; n = 7, N = 2; p=0.006) (Figure 5b).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data (p=0.006) and reference to Figure 5b.

claims.claim: A significant difference in the HYP during VOCs was observed after QX314 injection (baseline: −9.87 ± 0.75 mV vs. QX314: −2.19 ± 0.95 mV; n = 7, N = 2; p=0.003).
claims.source: While a significant difference in the HYP during VOCs was observed (baseline: −9.87 ± 0.75 mV vs. QX314: −2.19 ± 0.95 mV; n = 7, N = 2; p=0.003)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data (p=0.003).

claims.claim: No significant change could be detected in the HYP following antidromic activation after QX314 injection (baseline: −4.44 ± 3.57 mV vs. QX314: −4.3 ± 3.56 mV, n = 7, N = 2; p=0.703).
claims.source: no significant change could be detected in the HYP following antidromic activation (baseline: −4.44 ± 3.57 mV vs. QX314: −4.3 ± 3.56 mV, n = 7, N = 2; p=0.703) (Figure 5a, b).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data (p=0.703) and reference to Figure 5a, b.

claims.claim: The contribution of the recorded motoneuronal AP firing to the firing of that motoneuron is rather small during VOC activity (the activity of the neuron is dominated by gap junction-coupled potentials).
claims.source: These experiments demonstrated that (i) the contribution of the recorded motoneuronal AP firing to the firing of that motoneuron is rather small during VOC activity (the activity of the neuron is dominated by gap junction-coupled potentials);
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the QX314 experimental results.

claims.claim: During a VOC, the HYP amplitude of the recorded neuron only partly depends on its firing an AP.
claims.source: (ii) during a VOC, the HYP amplitude of the recorded neuron only partly depends on its firing an AP (also see above);
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the QX314 experimental results.

claims.claim: Most of the activity displayed by a given motoneuron reflects population-level motoneuronal activity.
claims.source: and (iii) most of the activity displayed by a given motoneuron reflects population-level motoneuronal activity.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the QX314 experimental results.

claims.claim: A combined superfusion and pressure injection of carbenoxolone (CBX) directly into VMN severely impaired the vocal network's ability to generate synchronized motor discharges as evidenced by barely detectable VOC activity.
claims.source: A combined superfusion of the exposed vocal hindbrain region coupled with pressure injection of carbenoxolone (CBX, a gap junction blocker) directly into VMN severely impaired the vocal network's ability to generate synchronized motor discharges as evidenced by barely detectable VOC activity (Figure 5c, red trace).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 5c showing the experimental data.

claims.claim: Upon antidromic stimulation after CBX application, APs had a similar amplitude as they did in controls (baseline: 17.80 ± 2.05 mV vs. CBX: 16.15 ± 2.14 mV; n = 25, N = 3; p=0.59).
claims.source: Upon antidromic stimulation (Figure 5d), APs had a similar amplitude as they did in controls (see violin plots in Figure 5d; baseline: 17.80 ± 2.05 mV vs. CBX: 16.15 ± 2.14 mV; n = 25, N = 3; p=0.59)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data (p=0.59) and reference to Figure 5d.

claims.claim: The loss of vocal-related activity during midbrain activation after CBX was not due to CBX impairment of motoneuron AP-generating capacity, but to decreased electrotonic input to the motoneurons.
claims.source: showing that the loss of vocal-related activity during midbrain activation was not due to CBX impairment of motoneuron AP-generating capacity, but to decreased electrotonic input to the motoneurons.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the CBX experimental results.

claims.claim: No HYP could be elicited in antidromic-activated motoneurons after CBX application (baseline: −4.79 ± 0.94 mV vs. CBX: −0.79 ± 0.97 mV; n = 25, N = 3; p<0.0001).
claims.source: No HYP could be elicited in antidromic-activated motoneurons (baseline: −4.79 ± 0.94 mV vs. CBX: −0.79 ± 0.97 mV; n = 25, N = 3; p<0.0001).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data (p<0.0001).

claims.claim: Gap junctional coupling is required to activate the HYP.
claims.source: This showed that gap junctional coupling is indeed required to activate the HYP.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the CBX experimental results.

claims.claim: SR-SIM imaging demonstrated dense, punctate glycinergic-immunoreactive labeling throughout VMN.
claims.source: SR-SIM imaging demonstrated dense, punctate glycinergic-immunoreactive labeling throughout VMN.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by super-resolution microscopy data.

claims.claim: Overlap of glycinergic signal with labeling for synaptic vesicle protein (SV2) revealed prominent boutons directly abutting motoneuron somata.
claims.source: Overlap of glycinergic signal with labeling for synaptic vesicle protein (SV2) revealed prominent boutons directly abutting motoneuron somata (Figure 6a–c).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 6a–c showing the microscopy data.

claims.claim: Glycinergic boutons were also observed on motoneuron dendrites within the contralateral VMN and VPN.
claims.source: Glycinergic boutons were also observed on motoneuron dendrites within the contralateral VMN (Figure 6d–h) and VPN (Figure 6d, i–k).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 6d–k showing the microscopy data.

claims.claim: These results demonstrated an anatomical basis for glycinergic release and inhibition spatially distributed across the entire somato-dendritic extent of vocal motoneurons.
claims.source: These results demonstrated an anatomical basis for glycinergic release and inhibition spatially distributed across the entire somato-dendritic extent of vocal motoneurons.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the anatomical data.

claims.claim: At midbrain stimulation levels sub-threshold to VOC compound potential induction, tonic membrane HYPs (on average −2.48 ± 0.68 mV below RMP; n = 7; N = 2) could be detected, indicating activation of inhibitory inputs.
claims.source: We observed early on that at midbrain stimulation levels sub-threshold to VOC compound potential induction, tonic membrane HYPs (on average −2.48 ± 0.68 mV below RMP; n = 7; N = 2) could be detected, indicating activation of inhibitory inputs (Figure 7—figure supplement 1a, left; magenta trace: subthreshold, black trace: suprathreshold)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 7—figure supplement 1a showing the experimental data.

claims.claim: Changing the chloride reversal potential by intracellular chloride injections via 3 M KCl-filled electrodes revealed a prominent inhibitory input to motoneurons during VOCs.
claims.source: We also found that changing the chloride reversal potential by intracellular chloride injections via 3 M KCl-filled electrodes revealed a prominent inhibitory input to motoneurons during VOCs as the membrane potential showed significant changes in the degree of repolarization compared to baseline levels (Figure 7—figure supplement 1b, blue arrow).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 7—figure supplement 1b showing the experimental data.

claims.claim: The HYP during VOCs was heavily reduced after chloride injection (baseline: −9.62 ± 1.34 mV vs. chloride injected: −1.20 ± 1.23 mV; n = 10, N = 3; p<0.001).
claims.source: The HYP during VOCs was heavily reduced (baseline: −9.62 ± 1.34 mV vs. chloride injected: −1.20 ± 1.23 mV; n = 10, N = 3; p<0.001) (Figure 7—figure supplement 1b, blue trace), thus indicating an inhibitory contribution to vocal behavior.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data (p<0.001) and reference to Figure 7—figure supplement 1b.

claims.claim: Antidromic stimulation still showed the HYP after chloride injection, however, at a reduced amplitude (baseline: −5.28 ± 1.95 mV vs. chloride injected: −3.30 ± 1.71 mV; n = 9, N = 3; p=0.093).
claims.source: Antidromic stimulation still showed the HYP, however, at a reduced amplitude (baseline: −5.28 ± 1.95 mV vs. chloride injected: −3.30 ± 1.71 mV; n = 9, N = 3; p=0.093) (Figure 7—figure supplement 1c).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data (p=0.093) and reference to Figure 7—figure supplement 1c.

claims.claim: After strychnine injection, no change in AP amplitude during midbrain-evoked VOCs could be detected.
claims.source: After strychnine injection, no change in AP amplitude during midbrain-evoked VOCs (Figure 7a) could be detected.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 7a showing the experimental data.

claims.claim: Strychnine abolished the HYP of motoneurons during VOCs (baseline −4.67 ± 1.88 mV vs. strychnine: 0.89 ± 1.88 mV, n = 20, N = 2; p<0.001).
claims.source: Strychnine, however, abolished the HYP of motoneurons during VOCs (baseline −4.67 ± 1.88 mV vs. strychnine: 0.89 ± 1.88 mV, n = 20, N = 2; p<0.001) (Figure 7a).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data (p<0.001) and reference to Figure 7a.

claims.claim: The HYP during antidromic stimulation completely disappeared after strychnine injection (baseline: −3.85 ± 0.86 mV vs. strychnine: 0.40 ± 0.86 mV, n = 20, N = 2; p<0.001).
claims.source: The HYP during antidromic stimulation completely disappeared (baseline: −3.85 ± 0.86 mV vs. strychnine: 0.40 ± 0.86 mV, n = 20, N = 2; p<0.001) (Figure 7a, insets).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data (p<0.001) and reference to Figure 7a.

claims.claim: These results suggested that glycinergic neurons, activated via gap junctional coupling, were responsible for generating the HYP during antidromic stimulation.
claims.source: These results suggested that glycinergic neurons, activated via gap junctional coupling, were responsible for generating the HYP during antidromic stimulation.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the strychnine experimental results.

claims.claim: Following strychnine injections, spontaneous VOCs appeared with similar decreases in motoneuron HYP amplitude not seen for spontaneous VOCs under control conditions without prior strychnine injections.
claims.source: Following strychnine injections, spontaneous VOCs appeared with similar decreases in motoneuron HYP amplitude not seen for spontaneous VOCs under control conditions without prior strychnine injections (Figure 7c).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 7c showing the experimental data.

claims.claim: The results imply that gap junction coupling between motor and glycinergic VPN neurons is sufficient to drive AP firing of glycinergic neurons.
claims.source: Since VMN motoneurons lack axon collaterals (Figure 1d), the results imply that gap junction coupling between motor and glycinergic VPN neurons is sufficient to drive AP firing of glycinergic neurons.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the strychnine experimental results and anatomical data, with reference to Figure 1d.

claims.claim: The interval between the first and second motoneuron AP significantly decreased following strychnine application (baseline: 9.61 ± 0.69 ms, strychnine 7.94 ± 0.69 ms; n = 10, N = 2; p=0.049).
claims.source: The interval between the first and second motoneuron AP significantly decreased following strychnine application (baseline: 9.61 ± 0.69 ms, strychnine 7.94 ± 0.69 ms; n = 10, N = 2; p=0.049).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data (p=0.049).

claims.claim: Variability of the interspike interval (ISI), as measured by the coefficient of variation, increased significantly after strychnine application (baseline: 4.90 ± 3.95%, strychnine: 13.54 ± 3.95%; n = 10, N = 2; p=0.009).
claims.source: Variability of the interspike interval (ISI), as measured by the coefficient of variation, also increased significantly (baseline: 4.90 ± 3.95%, strychnine: 13.54 ± 3.95%; n = 10, N = 2; p=0.009).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data (p=0.009).

claims.claim: Strychnine increases both frequency and variability of motoneuron firing that matches VOC output.
claims.source: Thus, strychnine increases both frequency and variability of motoneuron firing that matches VOC output.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the strychnine experimental results.

claims.claim: Spontaneous VOCs following injection with strychnine had potentials varying in width and multiple peaks, reminiscent of VOCs associated with weak VMN synchronization.
claims.source: Spontaneous VOCs following injection with strychnine had potentials varying in width (Figure 7c) and multiple peaks, reminiscent of VOCs associated with weak VMN synchronization (Figure 2b).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 7c and Figure 2b showing the experimental data.

claims.claim: The pattern of VPN activity directly predicts the pattern of VMN activity, the intervals of VOC potentials, and vocalization PRR.
claims.source: The pattern of VPN activity directly predicts the pattern of VMN activity, the intervals of VOC potentials, and vocalization PRR (Figure 8a, Chagnaud et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Chagnaud et al., 2012 and reference to Figure 8a.

claims.claim: Antidromic stimulation of the vocal nerve leads to membrane depolarizations (via electrotonic input) in premotor VPN neurons in the closely related midshipman.
claims.source: Antidromic stimulation of the vocal nerve leads to membrane depolarizations (via electrotonic input) in premotor VPN neurons in the closely related midshipman (Bass and Baker, 1990).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Bass and Baker, 1990.

claims.claim: Toadfish VPN neurons generate two depolarizing components, one before and one during VOCs, that might reflect motoneuron activity leaking through gap junctions.
claims.source: Toadfish VPN neurons generate two depolarizing components, one before and one during VOCs, that might reflect motoneuron activity leaking through gap junctions (Figure 8a, Chagnaud and Bass, 2014).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on speculation supported by citation to Chagnaud and Bass, 2014 and reference to Figure 8a.

claims.claim: During antidromic stimulation of the vocal nerve, VPN neurons showed small subthreshold potentials similar to VMN neurons indicative of gap junctional coupling, as well as APs at higher stimulation amplitudes.
claims.source: During antidromic stimulation of the vocal nerve, VPN neurons showed small subthreshold potentials similar to VMN neurons indicative of gap junctional coupling, as well as APs at higher stimulation amplitudes (Figure 8b).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 8b showing the experimental data.

claims.claim: Antidromic activation in motoneurons could elicit AP firing in VPN premotoneurons.
claims.source: Thus, antidromic activation in motoneurons could elicit AP firing in VPN premotoneurons.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental observations.

claims.claim: The latency of VPN APs (ipsi: 4.66 ± 0.01 ms, n = 3; N = 1; contra: 5.43 ± 0.16 ms; n = 3; N = 1) roughly coincided with the depolarization following antidromically elicited APs in motoneurons.
claims.source: The latency of these APs (ipsi: 4.66 ± 0.01 ms, n = 3; N = 1; contra: 5.43 ± 0.16 ms; n = 3; N = 1) roughly coincided with the depolarization following antidromically elicited APs in motoneurons (Figure 3a, magenta arrow).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 3a showing the experimental data.

results.result: Gulf toadfish produce two main vocalization types (grunts and boatwhistles) with PRRs of ~200-250 Hz. Individual VOC potentials arise from synchronous VMN motoneuron activity matched 1:1 with motoneuron action potentials, with variable amplitude reflecting different levels of synchrony and recruitment. The vocal network comprises VMN (amplitude coding), VPN (frequency/PRR coding), and VPP (duration coding).
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C7 describe the basic vocal system architecture and are well-supported by multiple prior studies (Tavolga 1958, Bass & Baker 1990, Chagnaud et al. 2011-2014) and figures showing the anatomical organization and electrophysiological correlates. These foundational claims establish the experimental system.

results.result: Prior work established that VMN motoneurons are electrotonically coupled via gap junctions, with ultrastructural evidence for gap junction contacts between motoneurons and VPN axons. Gap junction passable tracers lead to transneuronal bilateral labeling of VMN, VPN, and VPP, while impassable tracers only label ipsilateral VMN. A subset of glycinergic VPN neurons are transneuronally labeled with neurobiotin.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C14 summarize prior anatomical and physiological findings from Pappas & Bennett 1966, Bass et al. 1994, Chagnaud & Bass 2014, and Rosner et al. 2018. These are well-established background findings that motivate the current study's investigation of gap junction-mediated glycinergic inhibition.

results.result: Midbrain stimulation evokes graded membrane depolarizations in motoneurons that increase until AP firing occurs, coinciding with appearance of a strong post-spiking HYP and VOC potentials. The second VOC potential amplitude significantly exceeds the first (73.89±4.4 vs 36.6±4.1 µV, p<0.0001), reflecting less synchronous activation initially. First APs have significantly wider half-widths than subsequent APs (0.81±0.11 vs 0.62±0.06 ms, p=0.001). Larger, sharp-peaked VOC amplitudes correlate with synchronous firing and narrower motoneuron APs.
results.evaluation: Claims C15-C25 describe the basic electrophysiological properties of VMN motoneurons during vocal behavior, supported by intracellular recordings shown in Figure 2. The statistical comparisons are appropriately analyzed with adequate sample sizes (n=8-14 neurons, N=3-4 fish) and significant p-values. The correlation between VOC amplitude and synchrony is well-demonstrated.

results.result: Antidromic activation via the vocal nerve reveals motoneuron APs lacking the prominent HYP at threshold, consistent with intracellular current injections showing no clear HYP. Motoneuron AP and HYP amplitudes were significantly larger during VOC activity than following antidromic activation at threshold (AP: 29.13±1.48 vs 21.46±2.93 mV, p=0.024; HYP: -10.92±1.16 vs -2.95±0.70 mV, p=0.001).
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C28 establish a key observation that HYP amplitude differs between natural vocal activity and antidromic stimulation, supported by statistical analysis (n=12, N=5) and Figure 2c-d. This finding is critical for subsequent experiments investigating the network-dependent nature of the HYP.

results.result: Low-amplitude antidromic stimulation produces small depolarizations with shapes and latencies (3.54±0.28 ms) indicative of electrotonic coupling, confirmed by collision experiments. With increasing stimulation, antidromic APs invade motoneurons with shorter latency (1.42±0.31 ms, p=0.003 vs subthreshold) and show slow decay (τ1: 0.89±0.25, τ2: 7.76±2.48) but no HYP initially. AP and HYP amplitudes increase with stimulation strength until plateauing. Phase plane analysis reveals additional depolarization broadening after AP firing.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C36 demonstrate electrotonic coupling between motoneurons using antidromic stimulation and collision experiments (Figure 3, Figure 3-supplement 1). The graded recruitment and latency differences are well-documented with appropriate statistics (n=9-11, N=4). The observation that HYP appears only at high stimulation amplitudes is crucial for the network-dependence hypothesis.

results.result: Renshaw cell-like recurrent inhibition was ruled out as the HYP origin based on lack of motoneuron axon collaterals and rapid HYP onset. Dorsal root transection showed no difference in HYP amplitude during VOCs (p=0.8) or antidromic stimulation (p=0.117), excluding a motoneuronal collateral via dorsal roots.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C40 systematically exclude alternative explanations for the HYP using anatomical evidence (lack of collaterals from Chagnaud & Bass 2014) and experimental manipulation (dorsal root cuts, Figure 3-supplement 2). The statistical analysis (n=18, N=2) supports the conclusion, though the sample size is modest.

results.result: Contralateral antidromic stimulation reveals electrotonic potentials that can evoke APs with significantly longer latency than ipsilateral stimulation (3.47±0.16 vs 1.42±0.31 ms, p=0.004). Subthreshold depolarization latencies do not differ between sides, consistent with electrotonic coupling. Electrical coupling alone can drive AP firing independent of whether motoneurons belong to ipsilateral or contralateral VMN.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C44 demonstrate bilateral electrotonic coupling using contralateral stimulation (Figure 3). The latency differences are statistically significant (n=11, N=4, p=0.004) and the interpretation is supported by anatomical evidence that motoneurons only innervate ipsilateral muscle (Chagnaud & Bass 2014).

results.result: During contralateral antidromic stimulation, an HYP component is clearly distinguished that occurs independent of AP firing in the recorded motoneuron, emphasizing the independence of these two events.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C46 establish that HYP can occur without AP firing in the recorded cell, supported by Figure 4a. This observation is critical for demonstrating that HYP reflects network-level activity rather than single-cell properties.

results.result: Intracellular current injections fail to initiate APs in most cases even at high intensities (>5 nA), consistent with findings in midshipman. When APs are elicited, motoneurons show rapid adaptation with long pulses but no adaptation with brief pulse trains (<5 ms) up to 110 Hz. The weak repolarization capability and low excitability prevent sustained AP firing that would decrease synchrony.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C51 characterize intrinsic motoneuron properties using current injection (Figure 2d, Figure 3-supplement 3). The findings are consistent with prior work (Chagnaud et al. 2012) and demonstrate that motoneurons require external repolarization (the HYP) for sustained firing at behaviorally relevant frequencies.

results.result: The HYP appears only at high antidromic stimulation amplitudes, suggesting network-dependent activation. Combining ipsilateral antidromic AP (without HYP) with contralateral stimulation shows HYP amplitude increases as the contralateral potential approaches the ipsilateral AP. Similarly, moving antidromic stimulation closer to VOC-related depolarization increases HYP amplitude, demonstrating necessity of network-wide depolarization.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C56 provide strong evidence for network-dependent HYP activation using clever stimulation paradigms (Figure 4, Video 1). The graded appearance of HYP with increasing network activation is well-demonstrated and supports the hypothesis that glycinergic neurons require population-level depolarization for activation.

results.result: QX314 injection into single motoneurons caused small but significant AP amplitude decrease during VOCs (31±2.67 vs 27.27±2.53 mV, p=0.015) but much larger decrease during antidromic activation (21.92±7.16 vs 8.90±6.82 mV, p=0.006). HYP during VOCs decreased significantly (p=0.003) but not during antidromic activation (p=0.703). These results demonstrate that single motoneuron activity contributes little to its own firing during VOCs, which is dominated by gap junction-coupled potentials reflecting population-level activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C63 use QX314 to block sodium channels in single motoneurons (Figure 5a-b). The differential effects on VOC vs antidromic activity (n=7, N=2) support the interpretation that individual motoneuron activity is dominated by network coupling. However, the authors acknowledge alternative interpretations (insufficient QX314), and the sample size is modest.

results.result: Carbenoxolone (CBX) application severely impaired synchronized motor discharge generation (barely detectable VOC activity). Antidromic APs had similar amplitude to controls (17.80±2.05 vs 16.15±2.14 mV, p=0.59), showing loss of vocal activity was due to decreased electrotonic input, not impaired AP generation. No HYP could be elicited after CBX (-4.79±0.94 vs -0.79±0.97 mV, p<0.0001), demonstrating gap junctional coupling is required for HYP activation.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C68 use CBX to block gap junctions (Figure 5c-d), providing strong pharmacological evidence that gap junctional coupling is necessary for both synchronized vocal output and HYP generation (n=25, N=3, p<0.0001). The control showing preserved antidromic APs rules out non-specific effects on motoneuron excitability.

results.result: Super-resolution structured illumination microscopy (SR-SIM) demonstrates dense, punctate glycinergic-immunoreactive labeling throughout VMN. Overlap with synaptic vesicle protein (SV2) reveals prominent glycinergic boutons directly abutting motoneuron somata and dendrites within contralateral VMN and VPN, providing anatomical basis for glycinergic inhibition distributed across the entire somato-dendritic extent of vocal motoneurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C72 provide critical anatomical evidence for glycinergic synapses onto vocal motoneurons using SR-SIM imaging (Figure 6). The co-localization of glycine and SV2 immunoreactivity at boutons contacting dextran-filled motoneurons provides strong anatomical support for direct glycinergic input to VMN.

results.result: Subthreshold midbrain stimulation reveals tonic membrane hyperpolarizations (-2.48±0.68 mV, n=7, N=2) indicating inhibitory input activation. Intracellular chloride injection via KCl-filled electrodes reveals prominent inhibitory input during VOCs, with HYP heavily reduced during VOCs (-9.62±1.34 vs -1.20±1.23 mV, p<0.001) but less affected during antidromic stimulation (-5.28±1.95 vs -3.30±1.71 mV, p=0.093).
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C76 provide physiological evidence for chloride-mediated inhibition using chloride injection (Figure 7-supplement 1). The significant reduction in HYP during VOCs (p<0.001, n=10, N=3) supports an inhibitory contribution. The non-significant effect during antidromic stimulation (p=0.093) is attributed to network coupling, though this interpretation requires caution.

results.result: Strychnine injection abolished motoneuron HYP during both VOCs (-4.67±1.88 vs 0.89±1.88 mV, p<0.001) and antidromic stimulation (-3.85±0.86 vs 0.40±0.86 mV, p<0.001) without affecting AP amplitude. Spontaneous VOCs after strychnine showed similar HYP decreases. Since VMN motoneurons lack axon collaterals, gap junction coupling between motor and glycinergic VPN neurons is sufficient to drive glycinergic neuron AP firing.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C82 provide definitive pharmacological evidence that glycinergic inhibition generates the HYP (Figure 7a-c). Strychnine completely abolished HYP during both VOCs and antidromic stimulation (n=20, N=2, p<0.001) without affecting APs. The inference that gap junctions activate glycinergic neurons is well-supported by anatomical evidence (lack of collaterals) and prior transneuronal labeling (Rosner et al. 2018).

results.result: Strychnine significantly decreased the interval between first and second motoneuron APs (9.61±0.69 vs 7.94±0.69 ms, p=0.049) and significantly increased ISI variability (coefficient of variation: 4.90±3.95% vs 13.54±3.95%, p=0.009). Spontaneous VOCs after strychnine had potentials with varying width and multiple peaks, reminiscent of weak VMN synchronization.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C86 demonstrate that blocking glycinergic inhibition increases firing frequency and variability (n=10, N=2), supporting the hypothesis that glycinergic inhibition is essential for temporal precision. The statistical significance (p=0.049 and p=0.009) and correlation with VOC waveform changes (Figure 7c, Figure 2b) provide strong evidence.

results.result: VPN activity directly predicts VMN activity and vocalization PRR. Antidromic vocal nerve stimulation leads to membrane depolarizations in VPN neurons (Bass & Baker 1990) and reveals subthreshold potentials and APs at higher amplitudes (latency ipsi: 4.66±0.01 ms, contra: 5.43±0.16 ms). Decreasing latency between ipsilateral and contralateral stimulation leads to VPN AP firing, showing VPN activation depends on gap junctional network activation. VPN activation could lead to motoneuron depolarization and activation of gap junction-coupled glycinergic neurons that inhibit motoneurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C94 demonstrate that VPN neurons are also activated by gap junctional coupling (Figure 8). The recordings from VPN neurons during antidromic stimulation (n=3, N=1) show similar electrotonic coupling properties as VMN. However, the sample size is very small, and C94 is speculative about the mechanism linking VPN activation to glycinergic inhibition.

results.result: Gap junction-mediated activation of glycinergic neurons accounts for remarkable synchrony in motoneuron firing and contributes to pattern generation. The HYP, which cannot be elicited by intracellular current injection, is essential for generating vocalizations with high temporal precision. Electrotonic coupling of VPN excitatory neurons to glycinergic VPN neurons activates the latter, causing feed-forward inhibitory action. This inhibition repolarizes motoneurons (essential for repetitive firing) and generates a window of decreased excitability preventing misfiring, providing an essential mechanism for rapid, highly phasic acoustic modulations determining vocal PRR.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C117 synthesize the main conclusions from the experimental results. The evidence from pharmacology (strychnine, CBX), anatomy (SR-SIM), and physiology (antidromic stimulation, chloride injection) converges to support the hypothesis that gap junction-mediated glycinergic inhibition is critical for temporal precision. The feed-forward model is well-supported by the timing of HYP during natural vocalization vs antidromic stimulation.

results.result: Boatwhistles show greater stability of inter-pulse intervals than grunts. Results strongly imply glycinergic premotoneurons determine this temporal feature varying with social context. During non-breeding season, HYP did not appear during antidromic stimulation though present during VOCs, suggesting seasonal variability possibly due to connexin transcript expression changes observed in midshipman.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C101 make strong inferences about behavioral significance that extend beyond the direct experimental evidence. C102-C104 report interesting seasonal observations but acknowledge these were not quantified. The speculation about connexin expression (C104) is reasonable but unsupported by direct evidence in this study.

results.result: During natural vocal behavior, VPN feeds forward to VMN. Excitatory VPN neurons could activate glycinergic VPN neurons via electrotonic coupling before motoneurons. The authors hypothesize that the characteristic 'pacemaker' potential in VPN originates from motor-premotor coupling, with excitatory potentials from VMN shunted by feed-forward inhibition while inhibitory potentials travel through gap junctions to contribute to VPN patterning.
results.evaluation: Claims C105-C115 present a mechanistic model for feed-forward inhibition and motor-premotor coupling. While the feed-forward hypothesis is well-supported by timing evidence (C105), the specific mechanisms (C106, C113-C115) are largely speculative. The authors acknowledge they do not directly show motoneuronal activity back-propagating to affect VPN firing patterns.

results.result: The manuscript discusses broader implications: teleost families with soniferous behavior contain nearly two-thirds of actinopterygian species; gap junction-mediated glycinergic inhibition may benefit acoustic signaling in different fish and tetrapod lineages; similar mechanisms exist in Mauthner cell circuits; teleost auditory systems are adapted to temporal coding of PRR; call types differing in PRR indicate behavioral state and are distinguished by toadfishes; transmission distance is limited by frequency content in shallow water; and comparable mechanisms may exist in other vocal vertebrates and motor systems requiring high temporal precision.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C133 discuss broader context and implications, supported by extensive citations to prior literature. These claims appropriately place the findings in evolutionary, behavioral, and comparative contexts. The speculative claims about other systems (C97, C112, C132-C133) are appropriately qualified and reasonable extrapolations from the data.

results.result: Anatomical evidence for local activation within VPN comes from transneuronal labeling of local VPN neurons after filling an intracellularly-recorded VPN neuron with neurobiotin.
results.evaluation: Claim C108 cites prior anatomical evidence (Chagnaud et al. 2011, Chagnaud & Bass 2014) supporting local VPN connectivity. This provides anatomical substrate for the proposed feed-forward mechanism.

results.result: Both sexes of Gulf toadfish are capable of acoustic signaling. Both sexes produce grunts, but only males are known to produce boatwhistles.
results.evaluation: Claims C134-C135 describe basic natural history supported by multiple prior studies (Demski & Gerald 1972, Winn 1967, 1972, Remage-Healey & Bass 2005, Fine & Thorson 2008, Thorson & Fine 2002). This contextualizes the use of both sexes in the study.
